commands.heading: Commands (backend → device)
commands.hello: Sent right after connecting. The device replies with helloAck (identity, firmware, capabilities, lanes).
commands.intro: The backend sends these commands to your controller. Answer prepareRace and startRace with the matching events.
commands.ping: Connection and latency check; reply with pong.
commands.prepareRace: Close and arm the gate, enable the given lanes, and verify the sensors — without releasing the cars. Reply with raceReady, or error if a sensor is already blocked.
commands.reset: Return the device to its initial state. A reset during a race aborts it first.
commands.startRace: Release the shared gate once, take the monotonic start timestamp, and reply with raceStarted. Accept it only once per race.

connection.envelopeIntro: Every message — in both directions — is a JSON object with the same envelope. The payload object carries a type discriminator plus the fields for that message.
connection.fMessageId: Unique id of this message; use it to detect and drop duplicates.
connection.fPayload: The typed body: a type field plus the fields for that message.
connection.fProtocolVersion: Contract version. This document describes version 1.
connection.fRaceId: Correlates every message of one race; equals the heat id.
connection.fTimestamp: Wall-clock time the message was sent (ISO-8601). Not the authoritative race time.
connection.heading: Connection & message envelope
connection.p1: The backend opens one persistent WebSocket connection to your device and keeps it open. Commands flow from the backend; events flow back from the device the moment they happen.

diagram.caption: The backend is the WebSocket client and connects out to your Raspberry Pi, which runs the WebSocket server. Commands flow right, events flow left.
diagram.heading: How it connects

errors.duplicateCommand: A command was received again that must not repeat (e.g. a second startRace).
errors.hardwareFailure: A gate or sensor could not be operated or read.
errors.heading: Error codes
errors.invalidState: The command is not valid in the device's current state (e.g. startRace before prepareRace).
errors.sensorStuck: A finish sensor is blocked when it should be clear.
errors.unknownRace: The raceId is not known to the device.

events.error: A problem occurred; carries a machine-readable code (see below) and a message.
events.finishDetected: One lane crossed the finish. Emitted per lane, independently. elapsedNs is the authoritative time since the start.
events.heading: Events (device → backend)
events.helloAck: Answer to hello: device id, firmware and protocol version, capabilities, and available lanes.
events.intro: Your controller sends these events back. Race times come from the device's monotonic clock in nanoseconds.
events.raceFinished: All active lanes have finished or the timeout elapsed. results lists each lane's status; a lane that never finished appears with status "timeout".
events.raceReady: The device is prepared and the gate is closed; the listed lanes are armed.
events.raceStarted: The gate was released. controllerMonotonicNs is the shared reference all lane times are measured against.

example.heading: Python controller example
example.install: install the one dependency, then run the script on the Pi.
example.intro: A minimal WebSocket server your Raspberry Pi can run. It answers every command and emits the events; replace the sensor stub with your real GPIO reads.

intro.heading: Overview
intro.p1: This page explains how an external race device — typically a Raspberry Pi driving the shared starting gate and the two finish sensors — talks to the racing-manager backend, so you can build your own controller.
intro.p2: The backend handles the user interface, race selection, live display, and persistence. Your device handles the gate, both independent lane sensors, and high-resolution timing, and reports results in real time.
intro.p3: Communication is a small JSON protocol over a single WebSocket connection. The backend connects to your device as a client, so your controller runs a WebSocket server.

rules.heading: Timing & correctness rules
rules.r1: Race times must come from a monotonic clock in nanoseconds — never wall-clock time.
rules.r2: Measure both lanes independently; never assume they finish in the same order or at the same time.
rules.r3: Emit at most one accepted finish per lane and race.
rules.r4: Decide the winner from the measured durations and finishSequence, never from the order messages arrive.
rules.r5: Make commands idempotent: a repeated startRace must not start a second race — answer with a DUPLICATE_COMMAND error instead.
